_comment: CliniX 2.0 Presentation Library: Symptom-First Approach to Acute Neurological Deficit (Weakness). Reuses shared Skills as atoms and provides tiered clinical reasoning from recognition to neuroaxis localization and emergency actions.
title: Approach to Acute Neurological Deficit (Weakness)
subtitle: Acute hemiplegia, paraplegia, quadriplegia, stroke vs mimics, neuroaxis localization, and emergency triage

redFlags: Sudden onset focal neurological deficit (face drooping, arm drift, speech disturbance — BE-FAST / Cincinnati prehospital criteria)
Fluctuating sensorium or rapid drop in GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale) signaling expanding intracranial hematoma, cerebral edema, or uncal herniation
Signs of impending brain herniation (Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations; unilateral blown unreactive pupil)
Acute respiratory muscle weakness with Single Breath Count < 20 or forced vital capacity < 15 mL/kg in acute polyradiculoneuropathy (GBS) or myasthenia
Sudden back pain followed by rapid bilateral leg weakness, sensory level on trunk, and acute urinary retention (acute spinal cord compression — surgical emergency)
Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and focal deficit (bacterial meningitis, brain abscess, or herpes encephalitis)
vitalsPriorities: Capillary Blood Glucose immediately: Every patient with an acute neurological deficit MUST have bedside blood glucose checked immediately to exclude hypoglycemia, the commonest and most easily reversible stroke mimic.

Blood Pressure Management: In acute ischemic stroke eligible for thrombolysis, maintain BP < 185/110 mmHg. In acute intracerebral hemorrhage, cautiously lower SBP to 140 mmHg. Avoid sudden precipitous drops that compromise penumbral perfusion.
Airway & Respiratory Assessment: Assess gag reflex, swallowing, and paradoxical diaphragmatic movement; GCS ≤ 8 requires definitive airway control.

hyperacute_seconds_to_minutes: Acute Ischemic Stroke (thromboembolic occlusion of cerebral artery)
Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA - resolution within 24 hours)
Todd's Post-Ictal Paresis (focal weakness following epileptic seizure)
acute_hours_to_days: Acute Transverse Myelitis (idiopathic, post-infectious, or neuromyelitis optica)
Acute Spinal Epidural Abscess or Hematoma
subacute_to_chronic_weeks_to_months: Intracranial Neoplasm / Brain Metastases with mass effect
Subdural Hematoma (chronic or subacute, especially in elderly / alcoholic)
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS / Motor Neuron Disease)

cerebral_cortex: Contralateral hemiplegia with cortical signs: Aphasia (dominant hemisphere), Neglect / Hemi-inattention (non-dominant hemisphere), Homonymous Hemianopia
Faciobrachial predominance (Middle Cerebral Artery territory) vs Leg predominance (Anterior Cerebral Artery territory)
internal_capsule_subcortex: Pure motor hemiplegia: Dense, uniform weakness equally affecting face, arm, and leg without aphasia, neglect, or sensory loss (classic lacunar infarct)
brainstem: Crossed / Alternating Hemiplegia: Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy + contralateral motor/sensory hemiplegia
Midbrain: Weber syndrome (CN III palsy + contralateral hemiplegia)
Pons: Millard-Gubler syndrome (CN VI and VII palsies + contralateral hemiplegia)
Medulla: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary: dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner's syndrome, ataxia, crossed pain/temp loss)
spinal_cord: Paraplegia or Quadriplegia with distinct trunk sensory level, autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention, constipation), bilateral extensor plantars
Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemicord): Ipsilateral UMN weakness and dorsal column loss, contralateral spinothalamic pain/temp loss
anterior_horn_cell: Pure motor weakness without sensory loss, fasciculations, muscle wasting, mixed UMN/LMN signs (ALS / Polio)
peripheral_nerve_plexus: Ascending symmetrical flaccid quadriparesis with glove-and-stocking sensory loss, early loss of deep tendon reflexes (GBS, toxic/nutritional neuropathies)
neuromuscular_junction: Fluctuating, fatiguable weakness, diurnal variation, ptosis, diplopia, bulbar weakness, no sensory loss, preserved deep tendon reflexes (Myasthenia Gravis, Lambert-Eaton)
muscle: Symmetrical proximal limb-girdle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from squatting, combing hair), normal sensation, normal reflexes until late (Polymyositis, Dermatomyositis, Muscular Dystrophies)

discriminators.title: Cortical vs Subcortical (Lacunar) Stroke
discriminators.finding: Cortical stroke features higher cortical dysfunctions (Aphasia, Apraxia, Agnosia, Spatial Neglect) and unequal weakness (arm > leg in MCA; leg > arm in ACA). Subcortical capsular stroke shows pure motor hemiplegia equally involving face, arm, and leg without any cortical signs.
discriminators.highYield: Presence of aphasia or spatial neglect conclusively confirms cortical localization and excludes a simple lacunar syndrome.

discriminators.title: UMN vs LMN Facial Nerve Palsy
discriminators.finding: UMN lesion (supranuclear stroke): Forehead wrinkling is preserved because the frontalis muscle receives bilateral corticobulbar innervation; only lower half of face is paralyzed. LMN lesion (nuclear/infranuclear Bell's palsy): Entire ipsilateral side of face is paralyzed, including inability to wrinkle forehead and incomplete eye closure (Bell's phenomenon).
discriminators.highYield: If the patient can wrinkle their forehead when looking up, the facial weakness is UMN (stroke/central) until proven otherwise.

discriminators.title: Acute Stroke vs Todd's Paresis
discriminators.finding: Todd's paresis is transient focal motor weakness following a seizure. Key clues: witnessed convulsion, tongue biting, urinary incontinence, post-ictal confusion, previous epilepsy. Sensation is often preserved and weakness resolves within 24 hours.
discriminators.highYield: Never diagnose Todd's paresis without brain imaging: a seizure can be the initial presentation of acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke.

discriminators.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome vs Acute Transverse Myelitis
discriminators.finding: GBS causes flaccid ascending weakness with universal AREFLEXIA (absent ankle and knee jerks early) and no sharp sensory level on the trunk. Transverse Myelitis presents with a sharp spinal sensory level, early urinary retention, and extensor plantar responses (Babinski positive).
discriminators.highYield: Absent deep tendon reflexes in weak legs point to peripheral neuropathy / GBS; hyperreflexia and extensor plantars point to myelopathy.

dontMiss.disease: Acute Ischemic Stroke (within Thrombolytic / Thrombectomy Window)
dontMiss.clue: Sudden onset focal neurological deficit with known time of symptom onset or last seen normal.
dontMiss.action: Immediate non-contrast head CT to rule out hemorrhage, calculate NIHSS score, administer IV Alteplase / Tenecteplase if within 4.5 hours and no contraindications; immediate CT Angiography to evaluate for Large Vessel Occlusion (LVO) eligible for Endovascular Mechanical Thrombectomy within 24 hours.

dontMiss.clue: Bilateral leg weakness, bilateral sensory level on thorax/abdomen, saddle anesthesia, acute urinary retention, fecal incontinence, lax anal tone.
dontMiss.action: SURGICAL EMERGENCY. High-dose IV dexamethasone (if neoplastic compression), emergency whole-spine MRI, urgent spine surgery consultation for decompression within 24-48 hours to prevent irreversible paraplegia.

dontMiss.clue: Ascending quadriparesis, facial diplegia, autonomic instability (fluctuating BP/tachycardia), single breath count < 20.
dontMiss.action: Serial FVC monitoring (rule of 20/30/40: FVC < 20 mL/kg, MIP < 30 cmH2O, MEP < 40 cmH2O). Elective ICU transfer and endotracheal intubation before emergency respiratory arrest. Initiate IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) or Plasmapheresis. Corticosteroids are ineffective in GBS.

dontMiss.disease: Acute Intracerebral Hemorrhage with Mass Effect
dontMiss.clue: Sudden headache, vomiting, high blood pressure, rapid deterioration of consciousness, focal motor deficit.
dontMiss.action: Immediate reversal of anticoagulation if applicable (Idarucizumab, Andexanet alfa, 4-factor PCC, Vitamin K), cautious BP lowering to target SBP 140 mmHg with IV nicardipine/labetalol, urgent neurosurgical evaluation for hematoma evacuation or external ventricular drain.

step1_immediate: Bedside Capillary Blood Glucose (rule out hypoglycemia immediately)
Non-contrast Head Computed Tomography (NCCT Brain: differentiates acute hemorrhage from ischemic stroke)
NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) standardized clinical neurological assessment
12-Lead ECG (rule out atrial fibrillation, acute myocardial infarction, arrhythmias)
step2_urgent: CT Angiography (CTA) of Brain and Neck (assess carotids, basilar artery, and large vessel intracranial occlusions for thrombectomy)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Brain with DWI / ADC (hyperacute ischemia detection within minutes, posterior circulation stroke)
Urgent Whole-Spine MRI (if paraplegia, quadriplegia, or sensory level suspected)
Complete Blood Count, PT/INR, aPTT, Serum Electrolytes, Renal Panel
step3_confirmatory: Transthoracic / Transesophageal Echocardiography (assess for left atrial appendage thrombus, PFO, infective endocarditis)
24-48 Hour Holter Monitoring (detect occult paroxysmal atrial fibrillation)
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Analysis (albuminocytological dissociation in GBS, oligoclonal bands in MS, xanthochromia in SAH)
Nerve Conduction Studies & Electromyography (NCS/EMG: demyelinating vs axonal neuropathy, motor neuron disease)

examPearls.text: In the first 4-6 hours of an acute ischemic stroke, a non-contrast CT head is normal in over 50% of patients. Examiners frequently ask: 'What does a normal CT scan tell you?' The correct answer: 'It rules OUT acute intracerebral hemorrhage, thereby allowing immediate intravenous thrombolysis.'

Grade 0: Complete paralysis (no flicker). Grade 1: Flicker or trace of contraction without joint movement. Grade 2: Active movement with gravity eliminated. Grade 3: Active movement against gravity but not against resistance. Grade 4: Active movement against gravity and some resistance (subdivided into 4-, 4, 4+). Grade 5: Normal power.

An inverted supinator jerk (striking brachioradialis tendon produces finger flexion with absent supinator/biceps response) indicates an LMN lesion at C5-C6 combined with an UMN lesion compressing the spinal cord and disinhibiting C7-C8 flexors below.
